newsitem.title: UK: UK Ofgas sets Monday deadline for storage response.
newsitem.headline: UK Ofgas sets Monday deadline for storage response.

text.p: U.K. gas regulator Ofgas has given until Monday for the industry to respond to its unbundling proposals, a conference was told on Friday.

Patrick Hoare of British Gas Plc's TransCo storage division said Ofgas published its proposals for liberalising the market in three areas -- storage, connection and metering -- on August 21, and responses are due by Monday.
"Ofgas is going to turn the responses round fast" to give British Gas an opportunity to consider its position by October 7, said Hoare.

This is the date by which British Gas must decide on whether it will refer Ofgas' pricing proposals to the MMC, and chairman Richard Giordano said on Thursday that he was undecided on whether or not to do so.

In its August 21 proposal, Ofgas suggested two ways of regulating the storage unit, Hoare said. The first is to apply a "strong discrimination condition" to prevent TransCo from applying different terms for storage to different customers.
The second is to impose a price cap on TransCo, determining a maximum on how much the company can charge for storage for five years.
"TransCo strongly favours the first of these options," said Hoare, adding that senior TransCo officials were still canvassing the industry ahead of Monday's deadline.
TransCo operates seven storage facilities -- five Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) storages, one salt cavern at Hornsea in Humberside and the huge Rough facility, a depleted gas reserve in the North Sea.

Under an unbundled storage regime, TransCo will sell storage separately from its core business of transport, Hoare said, and shippers who book storage will become responsible for ensuring they hold enough gas to meet demand.
Storage available in Britain amounts to just four to five percent of annual demand, reflecting the fact there are quickly accessible reserves of gas available in the North Sea.

This compares with 21 percent of demand in the U.S., and "30 percent or more" in France where monopoly supplier Gaz de France faces questions of security of supply from Algeria and Russia, Hoare added.
